messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh's Burden

Rajesh Patel had spent forty-two years in the Coast Guard, most of them stationed along the Maine coast where he had learned to read the water the way other men read books. He was meticulous, methodical, the kind of officer who checked equipment twice and knew every protocol by heart. At seventy-eight, he had retired with a clean record and a pension, and for the first two years of his retirement, he and his wife Priya had traveled—they had seen their grandchildren grow, attended weddings, lived quietly in their home in Portland. Then Priya died suddenly of a stroke, and Rajesh, now eighty and widowed, found himself alone in the house they had shared for thirty-seven years.

The accident had happened on a clear June morning in 1994, during a routine training exercise near Casco Bay. Rajesh was supervising a young ensign, Marcus, who was learning to navigate a rescue boat through shallow water. The instructions had been clear: stay in the channel, watch for rocks. But Rajesh had been distracted—he had just received word that his father was ill in India, and his mind had drifted for perhaps thirty seconds. When he looked back at the instruments, Marcus had already turned the wheel. The boat struck a submerged ledge with a sickening crunch. Marcus was thrown against the console, his arm caught and shattered in three places. The sound—a wet crack like a branch snapping—had lodged itself somewhere in Rajesh's nervous system where it had lived ever since.

Marcus had recovered, eventually. A full investigation cleared Rajesh of wrongdoing; it was ruled a training accident, one of those terrible confluences of inattention and bad luck. But Rajesh had never quite believed the investigation. He had come to understand himself as a man whose moment of weakness had nearly destroyed another person's life, and this knowledge had calcified into a certainty: there was something fundamentally defective about him, a flaw in his character that made him dangerous. Even now, decades later, he carried the conviction that he was the sort of man who could hurt people, that his nature was corrupted in some essential way.

For years after the accident, Rajesh had managed by staying busy. Work had been his refuge—the structure, the protocols, the clear lines of responsibility. But retirement had taken that away. Without the routine of the service, without Priya's presence to anchor him, the old thoughts had begun to surface more insistently. The conviction that he was defective had metastasized into a constant hypervigilance. He had to be on guard all the time now, watching himself, monitoring his actions for signs of the dangerous man he believed himself to be. This vigilance had begun to reshape his life in subtle ways. When he sat in restaurants or his doctor's office, he found himself choosing seats near exits, positions where he could see the room and feel protected from unexpected threats—not because he feared others, but because he feared himself, feared what might happen if he were caught off guard.

The triggers had multiplied as his sense of danger had grown. Any natural environment similar to the bay where it happened—a rocky coastline, a harbor, even the sound of water lapping against a dock—would send him into a state of high alert. His body would tense, his breath would shallow. Talking about the future triggered something equally potent; when his daughter mentioned visiting next summer or asked him to make plans, a cold dread would settle in his chest. He had come to associate forward-thinking with the possibility of causing harm again, as though the future itself were a minefield he was destined to navigate badly. And sirens—the wail of an ambulance or fire truck—would transport him instantly back to that June morning, to the moment when the emergency crews had arrived and he had watched Marcus being loaded onto a stretcher.

When these triggers struck, Rajesh's mind would fracture in a particular way. The memory of the accident would return not as a coherent narrative but as disconnected sensory fragments: the smell of diesel fuel, the metallic taste of fear, the visual flash of Marcus's face contorted in pain. These pieces never quite assembled into a whole. When he tried deliberately to remember what had happened—to make sense of it, to perhaps forgive himself—the memory would slip away, becoming inaccessible, as though his mind were protecting him from something too terrible to fully know. Yet when the memory came unbidden, triggered by a siren or the sight of a rocky beach, it would arrive with overwhelming sensory vividness, feeling completely real across all his senses at once, as though he were living through the moment again rather than remembering it.

To manage these eruptions, Rajesh had developed ways of thinking that felt protective but were slowly poisoning his life. He would tell himself that the event had not really happened, or that it had not been as bad as he remembered—magical thinking that provided temporary relief but never lasted. He forced himself to think only positive thoughts, to reframe the accident as a learning experience, a necessary part of his growth. He tried to push the intrusive memories out of his mind, to suppress them through sheer force of will. These strategies would work for a while, creating a fragile calm. But the suppressed thoughts would accumulate, building pressure, and when they finally broke through—triggered by a siren, or a conversation about his daughter's upcoming vacation—they would arrive with even greater force, more fragmented, more overwhelming. The harder he tried to control them, the more they seemed to control him.

The threat monitoring had become exhausting. Because he could not trust his own judgment—because he was certain that his defective nature made him dangerous—he had begun to avoid unfamiliar places where he could not assess the danger. He would not go to new restaurants, new parks, new neighborhoods. He had stopped accepting invitations to events he did not know well. This avoidance had consequences he had not fully anticipated. His daughter had stopped calling as frequently; his son had stopped inviting him to family gatherings. When his doctor suggested he take up walking for his health, Rajesh had refused, because walking meant going outside, meant potentially encountering unfamiliar terrain where something might happen. Instead, he had begun taking risks in other ways—driving too fast on familiar roads, ignoring his blood pressure medication, eating foods his cardiologist had warned him against. It was as though some part of him had decided that if he was going to be dangerous, he might as well be dangerous to himself.

The cycles had tightened over the years since Priya's death. Each time a trigger activated his fragmented memories, the sensory reliving would feel so real, so present, that it would reinforce his conviction that he was fundamentally defective. This belief would then generate more hypervigilance, more threat monitoring, more careful selection of safe seats and safe routes. The avoidance of unfamiliar places would expand, narrowing his world further. And the maladaptive strategies—the magical thinking, the forced positivity, the thought suppression—would provide brief relief before the cycle began again, each rotation leaving him more isolated, more convinced of his own danger.

It was his daughter who finally pushed him to seek help. She had come to visit last month and found him thinner than before, more withdrawn. When she mentioned her son's wedding next spring, Rajesh had become visibly agitated, speaking in fragments about how he could not be trusted around family events, how something bad would happen if he attended. His daughter had recognized something in his words—a rigidity, a hopelessness—that frightened her more than any specific symptom. She had made an appointment with a therapist and told him he was going, and Rajesh, too tired to argue, had agreed. What he feared most was that the therapist would confirm what he already knew: that he was broken beyond repair, that the defect in him was too fundamental to fix. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to name it, was that perhaps—after eighty years, after decades of carrying this burden—there might be some way to understand that a single moment of inattention did not have to define the entirety of who he was.
